title: How do you do Kafka transactions in Spring (`spring.kafka.producer.transaction-id-prefix`, `KafkaTransactionManager`, `@Transactional` or `executeInTransaction`), how do producer transactions tie consumer offset commits to produced messages for read-process-write exactly-once, and why does a DB write + Kafka publish still need the transactional outbox (Kafka transactions can't span the database)?
shortTitle: How do you do Kafka transactions in Spring, and why does a DB write plus Kafka publish still need the transactional outbox?

s1_definition.profdef: Kafka transactions let a producer publish to multiple partitions and commit consumer offsets atomically, so a set of produced records and the offset advance either all commit or all abort. In Spring you enable them by setting `spring.kafka.producer.transaction-id-prefix`, which turns the producer transactional, and a `KafkaTransactionManager` lets you wrap work in `@Transactional` or `kafkaTemplate.executeInTransaction(...)`. For a read-process-write pipeline, committing the consumed offsets inside the same Kafka transaction as the produced output gives exactly-once between Kafka topics. However, a Kafka transaction cannot span a relational database, so a flow that writes to the database and publishes to Kafka is not atomic across both systems, and you solve that with the transactional outbox pattern.
s1_definition.analogy: A Kafka transaction at National Bank of India is like a sealed batch of outgoing letters plus a note saying how far we have read the incoming mail; either the whole batch is mailed and the note updated together, or nothing happens. That works perfectly when everything is inside the Kafka post office. But the bank's money ledger is a separate building, the database, and the post office cannot reach inside the ledger building to make both commit together. If you naively write to the ledger and then mail a letter, a crash in between leaves the ledger updated but the letter unsent, or the reverse. The transactional outbox fixes this by writing the letter into a special tray inside the ledger building in the same ledger transaction, and a separate courier later carries whatever is in the tray to the post office.
s1_definition.oneliner: Kafka transactions make produce-plus-offset-commit atomic within Kafka for exactly-once between topics, but because they cannot span a database you use the transactional outbox to make a database write and a Kafka publish reliable together.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kafka transactions let a producer publish to multiple partitions and commit consumer offsets atomically, so a set of produced records and the offset advance either all commit or all abort. In Spring you enable them by setting `spring.kafka.producer.transaction-id-prefix`, which turns the producer transactional, and a `KafkaTransactionManager` lets you wrap work in `@Transactional` or `kafkaTemplate.executeInTransaction(...)`. For a read-process-write pipeline, committing the consumed offsets inside the same Kafka transaction as the produced output gives exactly-once between Kafka topics. However, a Kafka transaction cannot span a relational database, so a flow that writes to the database and publishes to Kafka is not atomic across both systems, and you solve that with the transactional outbox pattern.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A Kafka transaction at National Bank of India is like a sealed batch of outgoing letters plus a note saying how far we have read the incoming mail; either the whole batch is mailed and the note updated together, or nothing happens. That works perfectly when everything is inside the Kafka post office. But the bank's money ledger is a separate building, the database, and the post office cannot reach inside the ledger building to make both commit together. If you naively write to the ledger and then mail a letter, a crash in between leaves the ledger updated but the letter unsent, or the reverse. The transactional outbox fixes this by writing the letter into a special tray inside the ledger building in the same ledger transaction, and a separate courier later carries whatever is in the tray to the post office.

**One line to remember:** Kafka transactions make produce-plus-offset-commit atomic within Kafka for exactly-once between topics, but because they cannot span a database you use the transactional outbox to make a database write and a Kafka publish reliable together.

sections.s2_technical:
A Kafka transaction groups a set of producer sends and an offset commit into one atomic unit identified by a transactional id. You start it, send records to any number of topics and partitions, optionally send the consumed offsets to the transaction, and then commit or abort. If you commit, all the records become visible to consumers reading with read-committed isolation and the offsets advance; if you abort, none of the records are visible and the offsets do not move. The transactional id also enables zombie fencing, where a restarted producer gets a new epoch and the broker rejects writes from the old, stale instance, so a hung former leader cannot corrupt the transaction.

In Spring you enable transactions by setting `spring.kafka.producer.transaction-id-prefix` to any stable prefix. That single property makes the KafkaTemplate transactional and registers a `KafkaTransactionManager`. You then run transactional work in one of two ways. The declarative way is to annotate a method with `@Transactional` so everything sent through the template in that method is in one Kafka transaction and commits when the method returns. The programmatic way is `kafkaTemplate.executeInTransaction(t -> { t.send("a", v1); t.send("b", v2); return null; })`, which begins, runs the body, and commits or aborts automatically.

The read-process-write exactly-once pattern ties consumer offsets into the producer transaction. The consumer reads a record, your code processes it and produces output records, and then, inside the same transaction, you include the input offsets so that the offset commit and the produced output are atomic. Spring wires this for you when the listener container is configured with a KafkaTransactionManager: the container sends the offsets to the producer's transaction, so either the output is produced and the input offset advances together, or neither happens and the input record is reprocessed. Downstream consumers must read with read-committed isolation to see only committed output. This gives exactly-once semantics for a pipeline whose input and output are both Kafka topics.

The crucial limitation is that a Kafka transaction is confined to Kafka; it cannot enroll a relational database in the same atomic commit, because there is no shared two-phase commit coordinator between the Kafka broker and the database by default, and distributed transactions across heterogeneous systems are fragile and slow. So if your flow does a database write and a Kafka publish, wrapping both in a method does not make them atomic: a crash can leave the database committed but the Kafka publish lost, or the publish sent but the database rolled back. The transactional outbox pattern solves this by making the only write a single local database transaction. In the same database transaction that updates the business tables, you insert the event into an outbox table. Because it is one local transaction, the business change and the outbox row commit together atomically. A separate relay process, often change-data-capture such as Debezium reading the database log, or a simple poller, reads the outbox rows and publishes them to Kafka, marking them sent. The senior nuances are that the outbox relay is at-least-once, so a crash after publishing but before marking sent causes a republish, which means consumers must be idempotent; that this trades atomicity across two systems for guaranteed eventual delivery with a small latency; and that Kafka's own transactions remain the right tool when both ends are Kafka, while the outbox is the right tool whenever a database is one of the two systems.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem at National Bank of India is that completing a transfer requires both updating the account balances in the database and publishing a TransferCompleted event to Kafka, and these two must never disagree.

Problem 1 — the first version did the database update and then published to Kafka in the same method. When the service crashed between the two, Rajesh's balance was debited in the database but no event was published, so the downstream notification and ledger services never heard about it, and the systems were out of sync. This is exactly the dual-write problem that a Kafka transaction cannot fix, because the transaction cannot include the database.

Problem 2 — the team needed the balance change and the event emission to be all-or-nothing. This is exactly what the transactional outbox solves: within the single local database transaction that debits Rajesh and credits Priya, also insert the TransferCompleted event into an outbox table, so both commit together.

Problem 3 — the event still has to reach Kafka reliably. This is exactly what a relay plus idempotent consumers solve: a poller reads unsent outbox rows and publishes them, marking them sent, and because a crash can republish, consumers deduplicate by event id.

The code will define a Transfer, an `AccountRepository` with balances, a `TransferService` that performs the debit, credit, and outbox insert in one local transaction, an `OutboxRelay` that publishes unsent rows to a Kafka stand-in and marks them sent with at-least-once behaviour, and an idempotent downstream consumer. The demo step is: run a transfer so the balances and the outbox row commit together, then run the relay, simulate a crash that republishes one event, and show the consumer deduplicating it.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__create_tables.sql (Flyway migration)
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    id          VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,
    holder_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    balance     DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0.00
);

-- Outbox table: event rows committed in the SAME local tx as the balance change.
CREATE TABLE outbox (
    event_id   VARCHAR(40) PRIMARY KEY,
    aggregate  VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
    type       VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
    payload    TEXT NOT NULL,
    sent       BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE,
    created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

INSERT INTO accounts (id, holder_name, balance) VALUES
    ('SAV2001', 'Rajesh Kumar', 1000000.00),
    ('CUR3001', 'Priya Sharma', 250000.00);
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  kafka:
    producer:
      transaction-id-prefix: tx-transfer-   # makes the producer transactional
      acks: all
    consumer:
      isolation-level: read_committed        # only see committed transactional output
      group-id: notification
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/bankdb
bank:
  outbox:
    poll-interval-ms: 500
```

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a transfer of fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh to Priya that must update balances and emit a TransferCompleted event reliably.

Step 1: The transfer service opens one local database transaction. It debits Rajesh from one million to nine hundred fifty thousand and credits Priya from two hundred fifty thousand to three hundred thousand.

Step 2: In the same transaction, before committing, it inserts a TransferCompleted event row into the outbox table with a unique event id. Because this is one local transaction, the balance changes and the outbox row commit together, so it is impossible to have the balance updated without the event recorded.

Step 3: The transaction commits. At this moment the database is fully consistent, and the event waits safely in the outbox table, not yet in Kafka.

Step 4: The relay runs, finds the unsent outbox row, and publishes it to the Kafka topic, which delivers it to the notification consumer. But the relay crashes before it marks the row as sent, so the row is still flagged unsent in the database.

Step 5: The relay runs again, sees the row is still unsent, and republishes the same event. This is the at-least-once behaviour of the outbox relay.

Step 6: The notification consumer sees the event id it already processed and ignores the duplicate, so the customer gets exactly one notification. The relay then marks the row sent. The final state has consistent balances, one delivered notification, and the outbox row marked sent.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka transactions make a set of producer sends and a consumer offset commit atomic within Kafka. In Spring I enable them simply by setting the producer transaction id prefix, which makes the KafkaTemplate transactional and registers a Kafka transaction manager, and then I run transactional work either declaratively with a transactional annotation or programmatically with executeInTransaction. The transactional id also gives zombie fencing through producer epochs, so a restarted producer cannot let a stale instance corrupt the transaction.

For a read-process-write pipeline where both the input and the output are Kafka topics, I get exactly-once by including the consumed offsets in the same transaction as the produced output. The listener container, configured with the Kafka transaction manager, sends the input offsets into the producer transaction, so either the output records are produced and the input offset advances together, or neither happens and the record is reprocessed. Downstream consumers read with read-committed isolation so they only ever see committed output.

The limitation that an interviewer is really testing is that a Kafka transaction cannot span a relational database, because there is no shared commit coordinator across the two systems and distributed two-phase commit across heterogeneous systems is fragile. So a flow that writes to the database and publishes to Kafka is a dual write, and wrapping both in a method does not make them atomic; a crash in between leaves the two systems disagreeing.

At National Bank of India this bit us when a crash debited Rajesh's balance in the database but lost the TransferCompleted event, so downstream services never heard about it. We fixed it with the transactional outbox. In the single local database transaction that debited Rajesh and credited Priya, we also inserted the event into an outbox table, so the balance change and the event committed together atomically. A separate relay, which in production is change-data-capture reading the database log, published the outbox rows to Kafka and marked them sent. The senior nuance I always add is that the relay is at-least-once, because a crash after publishing but before marking the row sent causes a republish, so the consumers must be idempotent, keyed by event id; this trades perfect cross-system atomicity for guaranteed eventual delivery with tiny latency, and the rule of thumb is that Kafka's own transactions are right when both ends are Kafka, while the outbox is right whenever a database is one of the two systems.

keyPoints: At-most-once: fire and forget — may lose messages
At-least-once: retry on failure — may duplicate
